Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Daniel Mercer was 51, a widowed school principal from North America who had spent most of his adult life being the steady one for other people. Before his illness, he was known at the school as organised, calm under pressure, and difficult to rattle. That certainty was stripped away when he developed a life-threatening medical condition that landed him in hospital and, for a period, left him dependent on examinations, procedures, and staff moving quickly around him. He remembered fragments of the worst part of it only with effort now: the bright clinical lights, the antiseptic smell that seemed to seep into his throat, and the sharp, unmistakable odor of alcohol swabs near his bed. When those smells were present, he would feel himself snap back into the fear he had felt then, as if the hospital were returning around him in the present tense. Even now, a whiff of alcohol-based sanitizer in a corridor or the sterile scent of a clinic could make his chest tighten before he had fully understood where he was.

What Daniel found most disturbing was that he could not reliably summon the event when he tried. He described sitting alone and attempting to picture what had happened, only to find the details slipping away as soon as he reached for them. Yet sometimes, without warning, the full emotional force of the ordeal came back with no clear picture attached at all: a wave of dread, helplessness, and disgust that seemed to arrive in his body before any image formed. At other times the memory did come, but not as a narrative. He would suddenly feel as though his body were back in the same position it had been in during the frightening medical episode, tense and immobilised in the exact posture he associated with the bedside. He found that experience deeply unsettling, because it made his body seem like something he could no longer fully command.

In the months after leaving hospital, Daniel began organising his days around the possibility of being caught off guard. Before nearly any interaction, whether with a parent at school, a staff member in his office, or a neighbour who stopped him after work, he rehearsed what he would say. He would go over opening lines, possible replies, and exits in advance, as though improvisation had become too risky. At school, he still presented as composed to students and staff, but he spent far more energy than before preparing for conversations he once handled naturally. He also started cutting off contact with friends and family, at first by letting calls go unanswered and later by declining invitations so often that the pattern became its own kind of silence. His widowed life made that withdrawal easier to hide, but it also meant there were fewer people insisting on his company. He spoke of it with a flat kind of shame, saying he had become “someone unrecognisable,” not only to others but to himself. The man who used to manage a building full of children and adults felt disconnected from the person he saw in the mirror now.

Daniel was most vigilant around anything that resembled the hospital world he had come to avoid. He kept away from hospitals whenever he could, declined to visit a colleague after surgery, and took a longer route past an ambulance bay near the school rather than risk seeing the vehicles or catching the smell that seemed to cling to emergency entrances. Even routine physical examinations became fraught. A scheduled medical appointment could leave him rehearsing for days beforehand, calculating what he might have to say to get through it, and whether he could postpone it without consequence. He did not describe this as stubbornness; rather, he seemed convinced that the body itself had become unreliable. He said he could not trust his own body anymore, because it had once failed him in a way that had not been obvious until it was nearly too late. That belief coloured the way he moved through ordinary life now. He checked sensations constantly, noting every flutter, ache, or change in breathing, not because he wanted to dwell on them but because he no longer assumed they meant nothing.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was exhausted by the effort of keeping his life narrowed to what felt manageable. The isolation had left him lonely, and the constant rehearsal had made even simple exchanges feel staged and unnatural. At school he could still perform his role, but it took so much preparation that his job no longer felt like the familiar work it once had. He came for treatment not because he felt ready to revisit the illness, but because he was frightened by how completely his world had contracted around it. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to feel like himself again — or at least like someone he could recognise — and to stop living with the conviction that his own body could betray him without warning. What frightened him most was the possibility that this narrowed, guarded way of living was not temporary, but the shape his life would now take.
